To the Members of the Maine State Legislature,
We are writing in strong support of LD 14 SP 27, "An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks." This bill represents an important step towards acknowledging and addressing the historical injustices faced by Indigenous Peoples in Maine. It would not only provide free access to state parks for Indigenous communities but also restore a connection to lands that hold deep cultural, spiritual, and historical significance.
The land that now constitutes Maine's state parks has been home to Indigenous Peoples for millennia. The Wabanaki Nations--comprising the Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, Mi'kmaq, and Maliseet--have long had deep, sacred relationships with these lands. This bill is an opportunity to right a small part of the wrongs of colonization and displacement, offering Indigenous Peoples free access to the very lands that were taken from them. In this way, it is not only a gesture of reparations but a symbolic act of reconciliation.
Free access to state parks would allow Native communities to return to areas of deep cultural and religious importance--where ceremonies, traditional practices, and teachings have taken place for generations. For Indigenous Peoples, access to the natural world is not just a matter of recreation; it is an essential part of spiritual and cultural identity. Many of these parks contain significant places for ceremonies, harvesting of natural resources, and the preservation of Indigenous knowledge. The ability to freely access these sites would allow for the continuation of cultural practices and the preservation of traditions that are vital to community well-being.
Moreover, such a measure would recognize the long-standing injustices of displacement and broken promises that Native communities have endured. Many of the parks in Maine were established on lands taken from Indigenous Peoples, land that has been subject to colonization and exploitation. Providing free access to these spaces acknowledges the historical wrongs while promoting a path toward healing and reconciliation with both the land and Native peoples' heritage.
Maine is not alone in recognizing the importance of such initiatives. Other states have implemented similar programs that have been met with great success. In Minnesota, the state offers free access to state parks for tribal members, even going as far as to return the land to the Indigenous Peoples in certain areas that were spaces used for religious ceremonies. This policy has been praised for strengthening the relationship between the state and Native communities, promoting cultural preservation, and allowing for a stronger connection between Indigenous Peoples and their ancestral lands. Similarly, in California, Native communities benefit from free access to parks, contributing to healing and community-building while fostering respect for Indigenous stewardship of the land.
These examples show that when Indigenous Peoples are granted access to their ancestral lands, it fosters a sense of belonging and responsibility toward the environment, one that is rooted in traditional ecological knowledge. It also serves as a statement of acknowledgment and

respect for Native communities' ongoing relationship with the land--an acknowledgment that is long overdue in Maine.
Supporting LD 14 SP 27 is not only a recognition of the historical connection between Native communities and the land now designated as state parks, but it is also a step toward justice. It is an act of support for Native Peoples and their ongoing right to practice their culture and traditions, while also contributing to the health of the land and the wider community. We urge you to support this bill and take action toward reconciliation.
Thank you for your attention and for your commitment to justice.
Sincerely, Ashleigh Dunn, Abigail Bagley, Leah Bradstreet, Nathalie Poulin University of Maine Orono, School of Social Work 435-339-3864 (Ashleigh Dunn)

To Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry:

We are the core staff of First Light, a collective effort across more than sixty non-native conservation organizations working to return land, access, and financial resources to Wabanaki people. As core staff, this comment reflects our combined individual experience and relationships. We are writing to express our support for LD 14, "An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks".

Last September, a group of non-native and Wabanaki partners gathered to share seafood and community on the beach at Roque Bluffs State Park. It was a beautiful afternoon. Partners from the Penobscot Nation and Passamaquoddy Tribe joined staff from First Light, Maine Island Trail Association, The Nature Conservancy of Maine, Maine Coast Heritage Trust, and others. Staff from the Bureau of Parks and Lands and Roque Bluffs State Park were incredibly welcoming and supportive of our gathering, from initial planning through to welcoming us to the Park. We were reminded that state parks are special places for people to connect with one another and the land. As organizers, we felt wrong asking Wabanaki people to pay to join a gathering in their homelands. In our case, First Light was able to cover the modest state park fee on behalf of Wabanaki participants, but we know not all people and organizations are in the same position. LD 14 makes real our collective understanding of Wabanaki land relationships and offers material support for Wabanaki people to access Wabanaki homelands that are now beloved state parks.

Our Roque Bluffs State Park story is just one illustration of our broader work. First Light is committed to increasing Wabanaki land access, whether through supporting Tribes to reacquire ancestral lands or building relationships with conservation organizations so preserves are available for Wabanaki use. We believe the restoration of Wabanaki land relationships is better for Wabanaki communities, non-native conservation communities, and the health of the land. However, our work has revealed many barriers- be they financial, legal, or cultural- that impede Wabanaki land access. LD 14 is important because it removes the barrier of cost, making state parks more accessible to Wabanaki people. Plus, LD 14 is a demonstration of the State's acknowledgement and respect for the fact that Wabanaki people have longstanding relationships and legacies of care-taking for the lands the state now holds. LD 14 is an important step towards supporting Wabanaki people to access these homelands. We urge the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry to vote "ought to pass" on this bill.

Thank you for your consideration.

Signed respectfully, First Light Core Staff Brett Ciccotelli, Peter Forbes, Otto Muller, and Eliza Oldach

I live in Bar Harbor and represent Maine Climate Action Now (MCAN), a coalition of fifteen nonprofit organizations from across Maine united by a desire to progress our state forward.

Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry
LD 14--An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Karen Blakelock and I am a policy advisor for The Nature Conservancy in Maine. I appreciate this opportunity to testify in support of LD 14, An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks.
The Nature Conservancy (TNC) is a nonprofit conservation organization dedicated to conserving the lands and waters on which all life depends. Guided by science, we create innovative, on-theground solutions to our world's toughest challenges so that both nature and people can thrive. We use a collaborative approach that engages local communities, governments, the private sector, and other partners. The Nature Conservancy has been leading conservation in Maine for more than 60 years and is the 12th largest landowner in the state, owning and managing roughly 300,000 acres.
Supporting the voice, choice, and action of Indigenous Peoples is key to The Nature Conservancy's vision of a world where people and nature thrive. Here in Maine, we continue to learn about the historical and ongoing injustices faced by the Wabanaki Tribes. We acknowledge the urgency of addressing these injustices and support meaningful action in this direction. Providing free access to Maine's state parks and historic sites is a small but meaningful step.
Beyond the bill in front of us today, we must continue to strengthen the voice, choice, and action of the Wabanaki Communities. TNC remains committed to supporting tribal sovereignty and forging relationships based on mutual support and trust. We do not speak for Indigenous Peoples, but by working together we can elevate their voices and priorities and advance our shared goals. Our work should aim to build rather than burden the capacity of our Indigenous neighbors and providing them free access to Maine's parks and historic sites is a step towards recognizing their long history and ongoing connection to all parts of our State.
We urge this committee to support LD 14. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

To:  Committee On Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry From: Nathan Davis, Ph.D., Sierra Club Maine Date:  February 4, 2025 Re:  Testimony in Support of L.D. 14: An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Committee On Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Nathan Davis, and I write on behalf of Sierra Club Maine, representing over 22,000 supporters and members statewide. Founded in 1892, Sierra Club is one of our nation's oldest and largest environmental organizations. We work diligently to amplify the power of our 3.8 million members nationwide as we work towards combating climate change and promoting a just and sustainable economy. To that end, we urge you to vote "ought to pass" on L.D. 14: An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks.
L.D. 14 would provide free access to Maine's state-owned or state-managed parks, historic sites, camping areas, and beaches for members of a federally recognized Indian nation, tribe, or band. This bill has bipartisan sponsorship and is similar to L.D. 25 of the 131st Legislature, which both chambers passed but which died on the Governor's desk.
Maine would join Minnesota as the second state in the nation to allow native peoples free access to state parks. Nationally, tribal nations are granted free access to parks where the tribe has historic or traditional presences, or where indigenous people are gathering for "non-recreational activities," such as religious ceremonies or community education.
It will never be possible to truly redress the genocide and displacement of the indigenous peoples who lived on the lands and waters we now call Maine, but we are heartened by and enthusiastically support recent efforts in this direction. This bill in particular implicitly acknowledges the deep connection between these physical lands and waters and the cultures that they sustained and sustain still. It is fitting and proper that we support this connection as we can, and as this bill does.
We encourage you to vote "ought to pass" on L.D. 14. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Nathan Davis, Ph.D. Sierra Club Maine Legislative Team member

To the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry:
I am a member of the Parish of St. Brendan the Navigator Episcopal Church in Deer Isle, ME. I write in support of LD 14, "An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks."
Our parish fully supports the rights of Maine native peoples on their own lands and the campaign toward sovereignty, which seeks to align their rights with those of the other 570 Native nations recognized by the U.S. Government. We take this position in accordance with the Episcopal Diocese of Maine, whose committee on Indigenous Relations has also offered testimony at the February 12 committee hearing. That testimony includes the following historical background:
"From 2007, the Episcopal Diocese of Maine has led the movement of Christian churches worldwide to repudiate the Doctrine of Discovery. In the 15th century, popes of the Catholic Church formulated the Doctrine of Discovery, giving the kings and queens of Christian countries the religious authority to seize any and all lands, which were not already part of the territory ruled by any other Christian monarchs. This doctrine was used by the monarchs of England and France to lay claim to the lands and waters that became the State of Maine.
"The Doctrine of Discovery became the basis of U.S. property law in the U.S. Supreme Court 1823 decision in Johnson v. McIntosh. This decision stated that the lands of what had become the United States were owned by the United States by right of succession to the earlier European discovery, and that the original inhabitants might have some limited right of occupancy, but had no rights of ownership. Over centuries of European and American expansion, known as Manifest Destiny, Indian nations and tribes were forcibly removed to reservations. In the case of Maine, this was done without getting the Congressional authorization required by the U.S. Constitution."
While the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980 allowed the tribes to buy back a small portion of the lands that were originally theirs, they could only buy back lands for which there were willing private sellers. The public lands now controlled by the State were not on the market at that time, and now the state has the right and duty to grant unfettered access, especially to state parks. LD 14 would allow members of the Wabanaki nations of Maine to visit and enjoy these lands. Fairness and justice would be served, at minimal cost to the State, by allowing this free access.
I urge members of the committee to recommend this bill as "ought to pass" to the full legislature.

An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks
February 11, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Andy Cutko, and I am the Director of the Bureau of Parks and Lands. I am speaking on behalf of the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) in support of LD 14, An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples
Free Access to State Parks.
Maine State Parks and Historic Sites currently allow free day-use access to senior citizens, children under five, Maine veterans, gold star families, and military service members on active
duty. Maine State Parks allow free camping to Maine Veterans who are 100% disabled. This bill would add free access to Maine State Parks and Historic Sites for members of federally
recognized Indian nations, tribes, and bands.
Since September 2020, DACF and the Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands have participated in the
First Light Journey, a collaboration between conservation groups, tribal representatives, and public agencies focused on expanding tribal access and stewardship of Maine lands. In conversations with other state and national park systems, I've learned that similar initiatives are
occurring across the country.
Because fees from State Parks go into the state's General Fund, this bill will have a fiscal impact.
If we assume tribal members currently use State Parks at the same rate as Maine's population
overall, we approximate the fiscal impact at 0.6% of overall State Park revenue, or $3 9,344. We
consider this impact minor compared to the benefit to members of federally recognized Indian
nations, tribes, and bands.
Thank you for your time. I would happily answer any questions now or at the work session.

Testimony in Support of LD 14: An Act to Provide Indigenous People Free Access to State Parks, sponsored by Senator Craig Hickman, Submitted by Doug Welch, First Light Island Access Working Group
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry: My name is Doug Welch. For the past four years, I have been working with the nonprofit group First Light to increase Wabanaki tribal citizens access to lands in Maine. I submit this testimony on behalf of First Light's Island Access Working Group, which is composed of representatives of 10 Maine nonprofit and public entities. For the past three years the group has been successfully working to increase access to Maine's coastal islands and other coastal properties by Wabanaki people.
Maine's state parks are cherished by Maine residents and visitors alike. By definition they are some of the state`s most beautiful and inspiring places, which led them to become state parks in the first place. But they hold an even deeper significance for the Wabanaki people. These special places have been sacred to indigenous communities since time immemorial, supporting both spiritual and practical needs. Waiving visitor fees to the parks for Wabanaki citizens would be a powerful act of recognition and respect, reaffirming their historic connection to these ancestral lands.
This Act would come at very little cost to the state of Maine: the loss of a small number of park entry fees whose budgetary impact would be negligible. This new approach would be consistent with traditional recreational uses of parklands. It aligns with similar policies adopted elsewhere, such as Minnesota, which now grants free access to Minnesota state parks for 11 tribal nations there.

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Agriculture, Conservation and
Forestry Committee, my name is Luke Frankel, and I am the Woods, Waters, & Wildlife Director and Staff Scientist at the Natural Resources Council of Maine (NRCM). NRCM is Maine's
leading nonprofit, nonpartisan membership organization dedicated to protecting the environment
on behalf of our nearly 24,000 supporters statewide and beyond. I am here today to testify in
support of LD 14, An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks.
This bill is identical to LD 25, which was introduced in the 131" Maine Legislature. LD 25
received broad support from the public, nonprofit groups, and the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry despite the minor fiscal impact to the General Fund through lost
revenue. As a result of this support, the bill received a unanimous Ought to Pass as Amended vote by this committee and then sailed through both the House and Senate. The bill only failed to be enacted because it was held by the Govemor upon the conclusion of the legislative session. We, like many others, believe this bill deserves a second chance to become law.
As an enviromnental advocacy organization, NRCM is committed to protecting, restoring, and
conserving Maine's environment. We conduct our work on the unceded lands of the Penobscot
Nation, Passamaquoddy Tribe, Mi'kmaq Nation, and Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, who have been stewarding the lands and waters that we now call Maine for generations. After a long
history of broken treaties, forced relocation, and genocide dating back to the first colonial
settlements in New England, the time to correct previous injustices is far overdue.
In the 66 years since NRCM was founded, we've worked closely with Wabanaki Nations on key
environmental issues such as fish passage and toxic contaminants in our waterways. We
recognize the invaluable role that Wabanaki knowledge-keepers have in protecting the woods,
waters, and wildlife of Maine. For this reason and to correct the wrongdoings of the past, we are
committed to actively using our voices, resources, and power to support the Wabanaki Nations in their pursuit of sovereignty.
Although providing free access to state parks may only be a small step relative to the magnitude
of the injustices of the past, it is an important one given the strong physical, cultural, and
spiritual connection that the Wabanaki people have to these lands. We should continue to remove
barriers that may be preventing Tribal members in Maine from accessing the land that was
unjustly taken from them as this bill does.
For these reasons, we strongly urge the Committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 14. Thank you
for your time and consideration.

10036028:
To: Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry From: Pema Lhundrup Date: Monday, February 23, 2025 RE: Testimony in support of L.D. 14: "An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks"
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry.
My name is Pema Lhundrup, and I am writing to strongly support L.D. 14: "An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks." As an international college student who currently studies in Bar Harbour, Maine I will never know as much about this land, its water and air as those who have lived here for centuries and yet I have much easier access to these parks and their resources then many indigenous peoples who have lived here with their families for generations. This inequality is not a coincidence but a horrific truth that reflects the dispossession of the indigenous people from their lands and the systemic injustices they face.
This policy is not just a great equalizer, it is a necessary step toward honoring Indigenous sovereignty, cultural heritage, and environmental stewardship of the original people of the land. Some might say this is a form of reparation, I say it is a form of justice. For generations, Indigenous communities have maintained deep spiritual, cultural, and ecological connections to the lands that now make up our state parks. Restricting their access through systemic barriers like entrance fees places unfair financial hurdles for these indigenous communities who continue to face historical displacement and marginalization.
Today in a world where environmental degradation is evident indigenous-led conservation efforts have demonstrated the importance of traditional ecological knowledge in preserving biodiversity and maintaining healthy ecosystems. Allowing free access to state parks would facilitate opportunities for Indigenous stewardship, cultural practices, and intergenerational learning, all of which contribute to a more sustainable future for our shared environment.
This would not be an impulsive piece of legislation as it follows strong precedence set by several states, including Oregon and Minnesota. These are states that have recognized the indigenous right not as a special privilege but as a restoration of land access to a people who have a long ongoing relationship with the land. Maine, with its deep history of Wabanaki stewardship, should follow suit and reaffirm its commitment to Indigenous rights by passing this bill.
I urge the Committee to take this deeply meaningful step by ensuring free access to state parks for Indigenous peoples. Doing so is a recognition of historical truths, a commitment to justice, and a step toward a more inclusive and sustainable future for all.
In the words of Martin Luther King Jr, "The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice."
Most sincerely,
Pema Lhundrup

Doing so is a recognition of historical truths, a commitment to justice, and a step toward a more inclusive and sustainable future for all. In the words of Martin Luther King Jr, "The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice."
Most sincerely, Pema Lhundrup

TESTIMONY RE: L.D. 14, An Act to Provide Indigenous People Free Access to State Parks On Behalf of the Episcopal Diocese Committee on Indigenous Relations.
Senator Talbot Ross Representative Pluecker
Distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry.
My name is Richard Farnsworth and I am here today representing the Episcopal Diocese
Committee on Indigenous Relations. This is a committee that was established by the Church to deepen our relationship with the Wabanaki of Maine and to stand with the Tribes in their pursuit ofjustice, to affirm their inherent sovereignty and to support the preservation of Native
languages.
L.D. 14 is a small step in the righting of a fundamental wrong, a step toward fairness and justice. The Commonwealth of Massachusetts, (until 1820), and then the State of Maine, took these State Parks, historic sites, camping areas and beaches from the original inhabitants, often by force. L.D. 14 would give the descendants of the original peoples of what became the State of Maine, greater access to a
portion of the land now controlled by the State, that their ancestors once occupied and depended on for
survival.
Beginning in 2007, the Episcopal Diocese of Maine led the movement of Christian churches worldwide to repudiate the Doctrine of Discovery. This was a dictum, established by one of the Popes of the Roman
Catholic Church in the 15"` Century, giving royalty in Christian nations the authority to seize any and all lands which were not already part of the territory ruled by any other Christian monarchs. That Doctrine became the vehicle whereby England, France, Spain and Portugal laid claim to the indigenous lands in
the New World including the land of the Wabanaki in Maine.
Over the centuries of European and American expansion, known as Manifest destiny, Indian nations and tribes were forcibly removed to reservations. In the case of Maine, this was done without getting the
Congressional authorization required by the U. S. Constitution.
While the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act allowed the tribes to buy back small portions of the lands that were originally theirs, restrictions allowing the purchase only from willing sellers, eliminated these state owned properties not available. LD 14 would open the door to allowing our tribes free access to
the lands that they could not obtain through the Settlement Act. We believe that fairness and justice
would be served at, minimal cost to the State, and as a step toward mending the relationship with the
State.

Testimony of Sarah Woodbury, Vice President of Policy and Advocacy, Defend Our Health In Support of LD 14, "An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks"
Before the Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry Committee March 11, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry Committee. My name is Sarah Woodbury. I am the Vice President of Policy and Advocacy for Defend Our Health. Defend Our Health's mission is to make sure that everyone has equal access to safe food and drinking water, healthy homes, and products that are toxicfree and climate friendly. I am here to testify in support of LD 14, "An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks".
Defend Our Health stands in solidarity with the Wabanaki people. Maine's indigenous communities are an integral part of the fabric of life here in Maine. The Wabanaki peoples historic and cultural connection to the land cannot be overstated. The displacement of the Wabanaki and theft of their land has disrupted that connection. They are the original stewards of the land and as such, should be given every opportunity to visit and engage with culturally significant lands without any financial barriers.
Maine will not be the only state that has taken action to allow its indigenous community free access to state parks. In 2022, Minnesota passed similar legislation to allow its 11 federally recognized tribes free access to state parks. In Minnesota it has had a very small fiscal impact on the state parks, around $25000 a year1.
Maine has much work to do when it comes to healing the deep wounds that European settlers and the state itself have inflicted upon the Wabanaki people. Allowing them free access to state parks is a tiny but significant step that can be taken to help the Wabanaki people connect with their ancestral lands. We urge the committee to vote "ought to pass" on LD 14.

Wayne Cobb Friends Committee on Maine Public Policy LD 14
FRIENDS COMMITTEE ON MAINE PUBLIC POLICY Committee on Tribal-State Relations 129 Chesterville Hill Road Chesterville, ME 04938
From: Wayne Cobb, 147 Allen Avenue #34, Portland ME 04103 Member, Friends (Quaker) Committee on Maine Public Policy RE: LD 14, An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Wayne Cobb. I reside in Portland, and I submit this testimony on behalf of the Friends (Quaker) Committee on Maine Public Policy, specifically our Tribal-State Relations Committee. I speak to express our strong support for LD 14: An Act to Provide Indigenous Peoples Free Access to State Parks. The Friends Committee wishes to thank Sen. Hickman for introducing this bill and the multiple legislators who have co-sponsored it.
Before European arrival, all of what we now call Maine was Wabanaki homeland. Quakers in Maine have long supported the inherent rights of the Wabanaki to self determination and the need for equitable treatment by the state. It is incumbent upon us as a faith-based advocacy group to support the Indigenous peoples of this land.
If LD 14 is passed, it will signify Maine State Government's respect for the unique connection that the Wabanaki have to the lands and waters within our state's borders. Passage would signal progress toward acknowledging the Wabanaki connection to the lands and waters, and honor the value of Wabanaki access and stewardship in traditional Native territory.
Just a few examples of state-owned or managed properties of historical importance to Wabanaki people are: the land on which the Colonial Pemaquid State Historic Site lies, which was home to Native peoples dating back at least seven thousand years; Fort Pownall in Stockton Springs, one of three significant forts that the British built on the major rivers in the Northeast to cut off the Native waterways to the ocean; and campgrounds within The Penobscot River Corridor, which contains over 60 miles of river access and 70 miles of lakeside, features that provided sustenance and facilitated canoe travel for the Wabanaki from time immemorial. Enabling free access for members of federally recognized Indian Nations or Tribes in Maine to historic sites, camping areas and beaches managed by the state is an important step in the process of land justice, a step toward recognizing the long history of the Wabanaki and their ongoing connection to all the lands and waters of our state. The Friends Committee on Maine Public Policy urges the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry to vote unanimously ought to pass on LD 14.
